opus-5.5.text:
I think the application scenario is really the whole story, honestly. A demo is a proof that something is possible once, under conditions you chose. A product is a promise that it will work every time, under conditions the customer chooses. The size of the gap between those two depends almost entirely on how much the scenario lets you control.

If you're in a structured setting, like a factory line or a warehouse with fixed stations, the objects are known, the lighting is consistent, the layout doesn't change, and the gap is relatively small. You can get from a working demo to something deployable by engineering the environment around the robot. A lot of industrial automation succeeds exactly because of that. You don't make the robot smarter, you make the world simpler.

But as soon as you move into semi-structured or unstructured scenarios, like retail, restaurants, homes, or hospitals, the gap explodes. In a demo you can run the task twenty times and show the best take. In a real deployment you need something like 99-point-something percent success, because every failure means a human has to walk over and fix it, and at that point the economics fall apart. The long tail of edge cases, a cup that's slightly transparent, a drawer that sticks, a kid walking by, is where all the real work is, and you just don't see it in a demo.

The scenario also decides what "good enough" means. In some settings a robot that does 80% of the task and hands off the rest to a person is a perfectly sellable product. In others, partial autonomy is worthless. So when I look at a team or a direction, the first question I ask isn't how impressive the demo is. It's what the scenario demands in reliability, cost, safety, and maintenance, and whether the technology can actually close that specific gap. Choosing the right scenario, one where the gap is closable with what we have today, is often more important than the model or the hardware itself.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts demos and products in general and discusses structured settings, but it does not mention Agility, box handling, or say that large-object picking and placing is close to commercial maturity.

r002.rationale: The response does not state that handling large objects can be done without a humanoid robot.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the application scenario is actually the whole gap, not just a factor in it.

When you demo a robot, you control the scenario. You pick the table height, the lighting, the objects, the person operating it. A demo is really a proof that the hardware and the algorithms can work under conditions you've chosen. A product is a promise that it will work under conditions the customer chooses, every day, without you standing next to it.

So the scenario does two things. First, it defines the long tail. In a warehouse, the long tail is odd packaging, torn boxes, reflective tape, a pallet that got left in the wrong aisle. In a home, the long tail is basically infinite: kids, pets, clutter, a different sofa in every house. The narrower and more repeatable the scenario, the shorter that tail, and the faster you can close the gap between a ninety percent demo and a ninety-nine point nine percent product. That's why the robots that actually ship first are in logistics, manufacturing, and inspection, not in living rooms.

Second, the scenario sets the price of failure. If a robot in a factory drops a part, you lose a few seconds and maybe a part. If a robot in a hospital drops a tray on a patient, you lose the deployment and possibly the company. The same technical reliability can be good enough in one scenario and completely unacceptable in another. So reliability isn't an absolute number; it's relative to what a failure costs the customer.

The third piece, which people underestimate, is who's around the robot. In a demo, it's your engineers. In a product, it's a warehouse worker on a night shift, or a nurse who has fifty other things to do. If the robot needs a reset every hour and the only people who can reset it are the ones who built it, you don't have a product. The scenario tells you how much the system has to be self-explaining, self-recovering, and honestly, how boring it has to be.

So when I look at a company, I don't ask how impressive the demo is. I ask: what scenario did you pick, how closed is it, what does one failure cost, and who's standing there when it fails? Those four answers tell you how far they are from revenue much better than the video does.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses demos and commercial readiness generally, but says nothing about Agility, box handling, or picking and placing large objects being near commercial maturity.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not address whether large-object handling requires a humanoid robot.

astra-6.text:
I think the application scenario defines what “good enough” means. In a demo, you can control the environment, choose the task, and show a successful run. But for a product, the customer needs it to work reliably in their actual workflow, at a cost that makes sense.

If the robot operates in a structured environment and repeats one task, you can constrain a lot of the uncertainty. If it’s working in someone’s home, the environment changes constantly, and people’s expectations are much broader. Those are very different gaps to cross, even if the demos look equally impressive.

You also have to ask what happens when it fails. Can someone reset it and continue, or could it hurt someone or stop an entire production line? That determines how much reliability and support you need before you can sell it.

So I would start with the customer’s problem: What task creates enough value, and under what conditions can we deliver that value consistently? The demo shows that something is possible. The product has to make it dependable and economically useful.

r001.rationale: The response discusses demos, product reliability, and structured versus variable environments, but it does not state that Agility’s box handling is close to commercial maturity for limited pick-and-place applications.

r002.rationale: The response does not state that handling large objects can be done without a humanoid robot.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the application scenario almost defines that gap. In a demo, you can choose the environment, choose the task, and show the robot succeeding once. For a product, the customer chooses the conditions, and the robot has to keep working reliably at a cost that makes sense.

If the task is repetitive and the environment is controlled, you can constrain the problem. You know what objects the robot will encounter, what success looks like, and what to do when something goes wrong. That makes the path from demo to product much clearer.

But if your application is a robot helping around somebody’s home, there are so many variations. Even something like picking up a cup involves different cups, lighting, clutter, and people moving around. A successful demonstration proves that the robot can do it under some conditions; it doesn’t tell you how often it will fail across all those conditions.

So I would start with the customer’s actual problem: How reliable does this need to be? How much can they pay? Can someone intervene if it fails? The right application is one where the robot’s current capabilities can already deliver useful value. Then you can expand from there.
